newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Socialists reassert conditions for euro.
newsitem.headline: France's Socialists reassert conditions for euro.

text.p: Opposition Socialists reasserted conditions for joining a single European currency on Wednesday and accused President Jacques Chirac of muffling Paris' voice in Europe by calling a snap parliamentary election.

The party also said that creation of a single currency from 1999 was a political decison that should not be clouded by dogmatic economic criteria. It said that neither France nor Germany would respect all criteria.

"We want the single currency, but with conditions," party spokesman Francois Hollande said after a first meeting of party leader Lionel Jospin and other senior members to plan the campaign for the May 25 and June 1 National Assembly vote.

Hollande said the early vote was damaging to France's influence in a current review of European Union institutions to prepare for enlargement to eastern and central European states that is due to be completed in June.
"Very important negotiations are under way in the inter-governmental conference...France will be unable to defend its interests because it is holding an election campaign," he told a news conference.
Chirac brought forward the planned vote by almost 10 months, saying France needed to prepare for the single currency due from 1999 from a position of strength.

The campaign would otherwise have coincided with haggling in early 1998 about which EU countries meet the grade for a single currency. Polls indicate the centre-right will maintain a reduced majority.

Hollande accused Prime Minister Alain Juppe of preparing a new bout of austerity and planning to enter the single currency without conditions. "When you enter without conditions you go in with the conditions of others," he said.
Socialist economic policymaker Dominique Strauss-Kahn said the Socialists wanted the single currency to "counterbalance American domination and help growth and employment."

"As far as the (monetary union) criteria are concerned, neither Germany nor France, to mention but two, will respect them all. A political decision will therefore apply, I hope," he told the daily Le Monde.

"Even if it's clear public deficits cannot be allowed to slip, there is no point making an unjustified dogma out of the three percent criterion," he said. Countries are meant to limit budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product.
The Socialists have laid down four conditions for taking part in a single currency:
-- the entry from the start of Italy and Spain, and Britain if it wants, to avoid creating a currency dominated by the mark.
-- the creation of a political counterweight to offset the power of a European central bank.
-- the creation of an EU pact of solidarity and growth to help create jobs
-- that the euro should not be overvalued compared to the dollar
Juppe's allies say the conditions mark a weakening in the Socialist commitment to the single currency -- of which former president Francois Mitterrand was a main architect.

Jospin said he would travel widely during the campaign. The Socialists plan to meet the Communist party on April 29 in a bid to work out a joint approach. The Communists say that they want seats in the cabinet if the Socialists win.
